articles.title: Why Prompt Filters Don't Protect Autonomous Agents
articles.excerpt: Prompt-layer security was built for chatbots. Your agents are not chatbots. For most of the LLM era, "LLM security" meant one thing: prompt injection. The attack was text in, text out. A user tricks t…
articles.body: Prompt-layer security was built for chatbots. Your agents are not chatbots. For most of the LLM era, "LLM security" meant one thing: prompt injection. The attack was text in, text out. A user tricks the model into ignoring its instructions, and the model says something it shouldn't. Filters that scanned prompts and completions for injections were a reasonable answer, because the only thing at stake was the conversation itself. If a filter missed an injection, the worst case was a bad answer. What changed with autonomy Agents don't just talk. They act. A modern agent loops: it reasons, picks a tool, calls an API, reads the result, and reasons again. Those tool calls are side-effecting.
articles.author: Matteo Tartaglia

articles.title: Making unchanged pixels transparent made my GIF 25% bigger
articles.excerpt: For a multimedia course assignment I'm writing GIF frames byte by byte, and tutorials keep repeating one trick: store only the rectangle that changed since the last frame, then mark the unchanged pixe…
articles.body: For a multimedia course assignment I'm writing GIF frames byte by byte, and tutorials keep repeating one trick: store only the rectangle that changed since the last frame, then mark the unchanged pixels inside it as transparent so the previous frame shows through. Some posts say this halves the file. I tried it on a running-horse GIF and the file came out 25% bigger than just storing the rectangles. That second step is the part I had misunderstood. The rectangle was mostly pixels that had not changed My main test file is a cartoon horse from Wikimedia Commons: 307×230, 8 frames, 16 colors. I first opened it and three other samples in ImgIng ( https://imging.ai/ ), the browser tool I use for GIFs, in Chromium 149 on an M4 Mac, to check the frame timings it read from the files.

articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady. What I Built Sometimes the hardest part of a task list is deciding where to start. I built SlothPlan AI, a personal planner that turns a messy brain dump into small, manageable steps—with breaks already included. You can type something like: Finish the project proposal today, 50 minutes; reply to emails, 15 minutes; book a dentist appointment, 10 minutes. With hosted Gemma configured, SlothPlan extracts task names, durations, priorities, effort levels, and deadlines. You review and edit those details before anything is saved. The planner then builds a daily schedule around your available hours and work budget. Its defining feature is Sloth Mode. Switch it on for: A smaller daily work budget.

articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady Code reviews are essential but draining. Reading every changed line of a junior’s or colleague’s PR, spottin…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built Code reviews are essential but draining. Reading every changed line of a junior’s or colleague’s PR, spotting edge cases, and explaining fixes takes focus that’s hard to find at the end of a long day, so issues slip through. Local AI PR Reviewer does the first pass for you. It watches your chosen repos, reviews every new or updated PR with a local open-weight model on Ollama, and posts senior-engineer-style feedback: critical issues, why they matter, and suggested fixes. It’s comment-only, free to run, and your code never leaves your machine. Demo Code abhisek247767 / local-ai-pr-reviewer A Python-based GitHub Pull Request reviewer powered by a local Ollama LLM.

articles.body: Value Added Tax is part of almost every business transaction in the UK, yet the arithmetic behind it catches people out constantly. Whether you are pricing a product, checking a supplier invoice or preparing a VAT return, you need to move confidently between net and gross amounts. Here is a clear, step-by-step method that works for any VAT rate. A quick reminder of the UK VAT rates The UK currently has three rates: Standard rate: 20% – most goods and services Reduced rate: 5% – for example domestic energy and some renovation work Zero rate: 0% – for example most food, children's clothes and books The formulas in this guide work for any rate; just swap in the right percentage.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 21, 2008: India launches its 1st mission to the moon with Chandrayaan-1
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year.
